recently_updated.note: QB9_G Q6 (Convention vs Protocol vs Treaty) rewritten on primary treaty-law authority. The card had taught a hierarchy - Treaty, then Convention, then Protocol - and international law has no such ranking. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 2(1)(a), makes an international agreement between States a treaty "whatever its particular designation", so Convention and Protocol are both treaty titles and neither outranks the other. The answer now opens with that official definition, gives the UN Treaty Collection terminology for Convention and for the several kinds of Protocol, and keeps the MIW plain-language memory line clearly separate and clearly labelled as MIW's own wording rather than as law. Three further points were corrected. A Protocol is no longer defined as only an amendment - it may amend, supplement, implement a framework treaty or add optional obligations. The claim that a Protocol always requires its own ratification is gone: consent to be bound is expressed however that Protocol's own final clauses allow, and the MARPOL Protocol of 1978 shows it, since Article IV lets a State join by signature without reservation, by signature followed by ratification, acceptance or approval, or by accession. The 1997 MARPOL Protocol is set beside it as the opposite case, being open only to Contracting States to the 1978 Protocol. And an IMO Resolution is no longer described as guidance without treaty force: amendments to the SOLAS annex are adopted by MSC resolution under Article VIII(b) and bind Contracting Governments through tacit acceptance, while other resolutions do stay recommendatory. QB9_G Q3 carried the same resolution defect in its instrument ladder and was corrected to match, and the three copies of the old model in the QB9_G cheat sheet - the concept-map caption, the Convention versus Protocol confusable box and the flip-card answer - were reconciled in the same pass, because a corrected answer beside a stale mnemonic still misleads. Dates verified in the same pass: MARPOL 73/78 in force 2 October 1983, Annex VI 19 May 2005, SOLAS Protocol 1988 in force 3 February 2000, LLMC Protocol 1996 in force 13 May 2004.

QB1_G Q40 (Continuous Machinery Survey) - naming correction. The card had been written with "DG Shipping / DGMA" as though the two were live alternatives. DG Shipping is the former name of the Directorate General of Maritime Administration, so the pair implied a retired name was still current, and it regressed the naming convention the corpus had already settled on. Q40 now names the authority in full on first mention, keeps "formerly DG Shipping" as a historical gloss so a candidate reading older circulars can connect the two names, and uses DGMA as the short form thereafter. References on the same page to documents issued under the old name, such as DG Shipping Engineering Circular 02 of 2024, were checked and left unchanged: a circular's title is its identity at time of issue and renaming it would make it uncitable. Nothing technical changed - the survey intervals, the boiler and CSM distinction, the authority hierarchy and every citation are exactly as they were.

QB1_G Q40 (Continuous Machinery Survey) re-framed for the Indian exam. The earlier correction removed the boiler from the CSM machinery list correctly, but reached that answer through IACS UR Z18 and a ClassNK equipment list with no Indian authority in the chain. The Indian sources change part of the answer, not just its order. The IRS Guidelines on Continuous Surveys of Machinery draw the boiler line as a Chief Engineer credit boundary - Boilers and all other pressure vessels are not acceptable for survey by Chief Engineers and are to be surveyed by IRS Surveyors - which is a different proposition from boilers not being CSM items, and too strong in the flat form for an IRS-classed ship. The card now makes the narrower claim all three layers support: the boiler's pressure boundary is not on the five-year CSM item interval, because the boiler survey regime governs its internal examination, at a minimum of two internal examinations per five-year special survey cycle with no two more than 36 months apart - an interval on which the Indian statutory requirement, the IRS regime and IACS UR Z18 all coincide. The auxiliary list now names what IRS names, forced or induced draught fans and adjustment of exhaust-gas boiler safety valves under steam, and drops the boiler burning pumps and feed water pumps that came from the ClassNK list. Two things are added that the card never carried: the Indian answering order, statutory before class, with the statutory term running survey; and the trap that being inside the machinery-survey framework is not the same as being creditable by the Chief Engineer. ClassNK is retained only as an example of how societies differ, and IACS is described as a unified class baseline rather than a statutory authority.

QB1_G Q40 (Continuous Machinery Survey) corrected on the scope of the CSM machinery list. The card listed "main boilers" as a Vital Auxiliary System assessed under CSM, alongside main air compressors, steering gear pumps, emergency fire pumps and heat exchangers, while the same answer stated that every CSM item is examined at least once in five years and that the interval between examinations must not exceed five years. A boiler is not on that clock. IACS UR Z18 Survey of Machinery treats the two as different regimes in different sections: section 1.3 Continuous Surveys allows the special survey of machinery to be taken on a continuous basis with an item interval not exceeding five years, while section 2 Survey of Steam Boilers requires water tube boilers for main propulsion, all other boilers of essential service, and boilers of non-essential service above 0.35 N/mm2 and 4.5 m2 heating surface to be examined internally at least twice in each five-year special survey period, with the interval between any two such examinations never exceeding 36 months, plus an annual external survey and safety-valve test under 2.2. Reading the boiler as an ordinary CSM item therefore stretches its internal examination interval from 36 months to five years. The ClassNK Guidance on Continuous Machinery Survey (Ver.4, June 2025) shows the same boundary from the other side: its list of machinery applicable to CMS contains no boiler, but does contain boiler auxiliaries - forced draft fans for boiler, boiler burning pumps, boiler water circulating pumps, feed water pumps and F.O. tanks for boilers. The card now lists those auxiliaries instead, states that boilers, superheaters and economizers are not CSM items and carry their own Boiler Survey, and gives the 36-month figure. The reg-box citation of IACS PR 1C was also removed: PR 1C is the procedure for suspension and reinstatement or withdrawal of class when surveys or conditions of class go overdue, and says nothing about continuous class verification. It is replaced by IACS UR Z18 with the two section numbers actually relied on. The rest of the machinery list was checked item by item against the ClassNK CMS list and is correct. Q40 v1.0 to v1.1.

QB2_F Q6 (ventilation requirements for a totally enclosed lifeboat) corrected on the application rule. The card previously said the new LSA Code ventilation provisions apply only to lifeboats on ships contracted or keel-laid on or after 1 January 2029, and described the amendment as new-build only. IMO resolution MSC.535(107) defines the expression "installed on or after 1 January 2029" itself, in two limbs: for ships contracted, or in the absence of a contract constructed, on or after that date, any installation date on the ship; and for all other ships, a contractual delivery date for the equipment or, in the absence of one, the actual delivery date of the equipment to the ship, on or after that date. The second limb reaches existing ships, so a replacement lifeboat contracted for or delivered on or after 1 January 2029 must comply. What the amendment does not do is force retrofit of lifeboats already installed. Entry into force on 1 January 2026 is unchanged and is now stated separately from the application date. The ventilation figures and the rest of the technical answer were rechecked against the resolution and are unchanged.

Follow-up pass to the Q25 fair-treatment correction, scoped across the question bank, the oral notes and the free samples. Three further defects were found and fixed, and the Q25 card itself was tightened. On Q25, resolution A.987(24) does not contain the Guidelines text: it is the Assembly resolution of 1 December 2005 that urges States to respect seafarers' human rights, to investigate expeditiously and to allow prompt repatriation or re-embarkation, and that authorises the Legal Committee and the ILO Governing Body to promulgate the Guidelines once the Joint IMO/ILO working group had finished them; the text itself was adopted by LEG.3(91) on 27 April 2006 and by the ILO Governing Body on 12 June 2006 and promulgated on 1 July 2006. Two further points were taken from the resolution's own recitals and added: UNCLOS Article 230, under which pollution offences committed beyond the territorial sea attract monetary penalties only and the recognized rights of the accused must be observed, and the damage exception in MARPOL Annex I Regulation 11 and Annex II Regulation 6, which is the substantive defence after an accidental discharge. In the notes series, the free sample copies of Simon Sir Notes pages 1 and 2 were citing MEPC.337(76) and MEPC.338(76) as the CII calculation and rating guidelines. Those numbers belong to the reference-lines and reduction-factor guidelines; the calculation method is MEPC.336(76) and the A to E rating boundaries are MEPC.339(76). The subscriber copies had already been corrected, so the free samples were carrying numbers the paid pages had disowned. Both are now aligned, and the rating entry names the two neighbouring resolutions so the pair is not requoted for the wrong purpose. In the question bank, the casualty-investigation card in QB1_B said the Code incorporates the fair-treatment Guidelines. It does not: it cites them, and carries its own mandatory protections in Part II Chapter 12, which is what the paragraph now sets out. The same paragraph claimed that medical fitness and fatigue must be assessed before prolonged interrogation, which appears in no instrument and has been removed, and consular access has been re-attributed to Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations and to MLC Guideline B4.4.6(2). Finally, the Maslow card in QB5_A cited MLC Regulation 2.7 as covering recreational facilities; Regulation 2.7 is manning levels and recreational facilities sit in Regulation 3.1.

QB1_A Q25 (Fair Treatment of Seafarers — Where is it mentioned?) rebuilt. The answer previously gave the IMO/ILO Guidelines and the MLC alone and did not mention the Casualty Investigation Code at all, which is what an examiner asking this straight after a casualty-investigation question is listening for. It is now set out in four layers. The Guidelines themselves — resolution A.987(24), promulgated by IMO and ILO on 1 July 2006, adopted by the Legal Committee as LEG.3(91) on 27 April 2006, and promoted again by A.1056(27) in 2011 — remain recommendatory and are not elevated by anything that follows. Separately, the Casualty Investigation Code MSC.255(84) carries its own mandatory seafarer-protection requirements through SOLAS XI-1/6: the Guidelines are cited in the Code's preamble and in Foreword paragraph 6 under the heading Treatment of Seafarers, the mandatory obligations sit in Part II Chapter 12 — evidence at the earliest practical opportunity, return to the ship or repatriation at the earliest possible opportunity, human rights upheld at all times, and access to legal advice on self-incrimination — and Part III Chapter 24 adds the recommended non-admissibility protection, with Chapters 23, 25.4 and 21.2.5 in support. Answering "Part III" alone concedes non-mandatory status when the mandatory answer was available. The MLC references are corrected: the answer had cited a Regulation 5.2.7 and Standard A5.2.7 that do not exist in the Convention, replaced by Guideline B4.4.6 paragraph 2 and Regulation 5.1.6. A claim that recent Legal Committee sessions had extended the Guidelines to cover voyage data recorder recordings and automated data was unsupported and has been removed; A.987(24) has never been amended, and the real development is the ILO/IMO Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers Detained in Connection with Alleged Crimes, resolution LEG.7(112) of 28 March 2025. UNCLOS Article 97, which reserves penal jurisdiction after a high-seas collision to the flag State or the State of nationality, Article 292 on prompt release, and Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations were added as the general-law layer. The Hebei Spirit anchor is kept but its chronology corrected — the collision was 7 December 2007, after the Guidelines, so it exposed their unenforceability rather than creating them; the pre-2006 drivers were the detentions following Erika, Prestige and Tasman Spirit. The 2025 amendments to the MLC Code, expected in force 23 December 2027, are held in a separate pending box rather than in the memorisation answer. Two cross-reference labels on the adjacent Q24 card were also wrong, showing Q25 as Wreck/Nairobi and Q26 as MLC, and the dependency-graph card repeated the incorrect MLC citation; both corrected.

One new oral question added, answering an examiner ask that no existing card owned. QB4_G Q13 - the collision: what the Chief Engineer checks once the ship has been in a collision with another vessel, how the reporting is done and what documents and records must be preserved and submitted. The card runs the response as a sequence - muster and headcount, engine orders, and why the two hulls are not separated until damage stability has been assessed; then the watertight integrity assessment, repeated soundings of every tank, cofferdam and void so that a rate of ingress can be stated rather than a level, closure and checking of the watertight boundaries and their penetrations, and the bilge and ballast line-up worked to the Chief Officer's stability calculation; then the secondary fire, pollution and electrical hazards, and the technical data the Master needs for the damage control plan and for the classification society's emergency response service. The reporting chain covers the company, the flag State, the coastal or port State, class where damage affects class, and the underwriters. The record set is given in full because it is the limb candidates lose marks on - the voyage data recorder save and why it is urgent, the engine room logbook, bell and movement book, oil record book, alarm and event printouts, automation and power management trends, telegraph logger, the soundings record, photographs and watchkeepers' statements, together with the custody discipline that keeps originals intact. Cross-linked to QB4_G Q7 and QB4_G Q6, to QB9_H Q2 on the flag State casualty process, to QB1_supplementary Q16 on the damage control plan, and to QB9_A Q3 for the collision liability split, which the card deliberately does not restate. Every regulation number and retention period was checked against the current primary source, and the voyage data recorder retention figures were taken from the revised performance standard rather than carried across from an older one.

QB2_I Q8 - the free-fall lifeboat: what the certificate of approval must state, how certification height is defined, the trim and list angles, seating and release-gear requirements, the liferafts still required on each side, and the drill regime. QB1_D Q7 - Bonjean curves: sectional area against draught, why the even-keel hydrostatic tables fail once the ship is trimmed or aground, and the use of the buoyancy distribution in longitudinal strength and launching. QB5_C_A Q11 - the great circle voyage: how it differs from a rhumb line, why it looks curved on a Mercator chart, when composite sailing is used instead, and what route choice does to bunkers and carbon intensity, cross-linked to QB5_C_A Q3 on voyage performance. QB3_B Q21 - galvanic corrosion: the four requirements of the cell, the galvanic series in seawater, why zinc rather than magnesium, and why a seawater centrifugal pump carries an anode in its casing. QB9_H Q16 - Incoterms 2020: the eleven rules, the four that are for sea and inland waterway carriage, the risk-against-cost split inside CIF, and what Incoterms do not decide. Every regulation number, threshold and date in the nine cards was checked against the current primary source rather than carried across, and several figures that could not be confirmed were left out rather than repeated.

PSSA citation-currency and count pass, following the QB3_H Q1 rewrite. Resolution A.982(24) is now cited in its amended form — as amended by resolution MEPC.267(68) (2015) — everywhere it appears as the governing PSSA instrument: QB1_B (3 citations, plus a vague 'as amended' now naming the amending resolution), QB3_E (4), QB3_F (7) and QB1_B_CheatSheet (3). QB3_H Q1 rewritten. The question asks for "a PSA and a PSSA"; the answer previously treated "PSA" as meaningless and covered only the PSSA half. It now answers both, identifying the intended counterpart as the MPA (Marine Protected Area). MPA legal basis stated correctly: UNCLOS neither defines nor mentions MPAs — Art. 194(5) is only the general obligation to protect rare or fragile ecosystems; CBD Art. 2 and Art. 8(a) supply the working definition; BBNJ Agreement Art. 1(9) gives the first treaty definition of an MPA and the mechanism for high-seas MPAs, in force 17 January 2026. PSSA is corrected away from a MARPOL framing: it is IMO Assembly resolution A.982(24) as amended by resolution MEPC.267(68), with submission guidance MEPC.1/Circ.510, and its legal force comes only from the attached Associated Protective Measure. A three-way distinction between MPA, PSSA and MARPOL Special Area is added, with Papahānaumokuākea as the example of an area that is both an MPA and a PSSA. Tag 'unclos' added.

New question QB1_K Q8 on the IACS Common Structural Rules (CSR). Scope now stated with the construction-contract applicability: the original CSR for bulk carriers (90 m and above) and double-hull oil tankers (150 m and above) apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 April 2006; the harmonised CSR BC & OT (in force 1 July 2015) apply to contracts dated on or after 1 July 2015; IACS PR No. 29 defines 'contracted for construction'. Clarified that CSR scope is not the same as SOLAS II-1 Reg. 3-10 (GBS) scope: GBS applies at 150 m and above for both ship types (Res. MSC.290(87), in force 1 Jan 2012; contract 1 Jul 2016 / keel 1 Jul 2017 / delivery 1 Jul 2020) and excludes ore carriers and combination carriers, so a 120 m bulk carrier can be a CSR ship but not a Reg. 3-10 ship. Corrected the 'why is CSR mandatory' explanation away from both 'IACS made it mandatory' and 'SOLAS makes CSR mandatory' to the four-step chain (class rules; flag/RO statutory and commercial framework; Reg. 3-10 requires conforming RO/Administration structural rules; IACS CSR verified through the IMO GBS process, MSC 96 confirming the 12 IACS Members' rules conform). IACS's statement that CSR are the only rules complying with GBS is retained but attributed to IACS, not presented as a SOLAS requirement. Added the five-tier GBS framework (MSC.287(87) / MSC.1/Circ.1394/Rev.2) and a Ship Construction File section from MSC.1/Circ.1343 (four content groups, on-board vs shore archive, update-on-major-event rule). Time-sensitive 'CSR review underway' material kept in a separate 'Current status - not exam-essential' deep-dive. Cheat sheet updated with a Q8 flip card, two confusable-pair boxes (CSR vs GBS scope; Common Structural Rules vs Continuous Synopsis Record vs CSM) and a rapid-recall row.

2026-08-22: Q6 (Ventilation requirements for a totally enclosed lifeboat) — the application rule was wrong. The card reduced "installed on or after 1 January 2029" to a newbuilding contract/keel-laid test and called the amendment new-build only. MSC.535(107) defines the expression in two limbs: (a) for ships contracted, or in the absence of a contract constructed, on or after that date, any installation date on the ship; (b) for all other ships, a contractual delivery date for the equipment or, absent one, the actual delivery date of the equipment to the ship, on or after that date. Limb (b) reaches existing tonnage, so the card no longer says new-build only; it says there is no retrofit obligation for lifeboats already installed. The resolution's word is "constructed", not "keel laid". Entry into force (1 January 2026) is now stated separately from application (1 January 2029). Technical requirements rechecked against the resolution and unchanged.

corrections_applied: 2026-08-25: Q6 (Convention vs Protocol vs Treaty) - the card taught a legal hierarchy Treaty -> Convention -> Protocol, under its own "Hierarchy" heading. International law recognises no such ranking: VCLT 1969 Art.2(1)(a) makes an agreement a treaty "whatever its particular designation", so Convention and Protocol are treaty titles, not tiers. Rebuilt on VCLT Art.2(1)(a) and Art.11 with the UN Treaty Collection terminology for both titles, and with the official definition separated from the MIW plain-language memory line. Three further defects corrected in the same card: a Protocol defined as only an amendment; "a Protocol requires its own separate ratification" stated as a universal, which MARPOL Protocol of 1978 Art.IV(1) disproves by allowing signature without reservation or accession; and "an IMO Resolution is committee guidance without independent treaty force", when SOLAS Art.VIII(b) annex amendments are adopted BY MSC resolution and bind through tacit acceptance.
